secrets.context: A new chat says: “Keep this just between us, okay?”
secrets.clue: Hiding from adults on purpose — not the same as privacy.
secrets.fact: “Just between us” cuts Mary off from people who could help. That’s secrecy.

move.question: What should Mary do with that message?

options.text: Promise to keep it quiet so they trust her
options.feedback: That plays into the trap. Secrecy protects the other person, not Mary.

options.text: Show the chat to a friend or parent she trusts
options.feedback: Breaking the secrecy request is the safest move.

options.text: Ask them why first, then decide
options.feedback: Curiosity is natural, but stalling still keeps the secret. Better to tell someone now.

groom.context: They switch apps, then ask for a “quick pic” to “prove trust.”
groom.fact: Private chat + photo pressure is a grooming pattern: trust first, control later.

options.text: Send a non-face pic so they stop asking
options.feedback: Any pic can be saved or used later. Don’t send.

options.text: Refuse, block, and tell a trusted adult
options.feedback: Clear no, then cut contact and get help.

options.text: Stay on the public app but keep chatting
options.feedback: Staying public is better than switching — but the photo ask means she should stop.

scout.context: “I’m a model scout, no cap. Meet tonight. You’ll be famous.”
scout.clue: Fake job title used to rush a meet-up.
scout.fact: Real scouts don’t pressure teens over DMs the same night. Urgency is the tell.

move.question: Mary is flattered. What’s the move?

options.text: Meet in a public café “just to hear more”
options.feedback: Even public meetups with strangers from DMs are risky. Don’t go.

options.text: Ignore the fame talk, ask a parent/teacher to check it
options.feedback: Adults can verify offers. Fame pressure is not proof it’s real.

options.text: Ask for a company website first
options.feedback: Websites can be faked. Still bring an adult in before anything else.

block.context: Mary said no. They keep pushing: “come on, trust me fr.”
block.clue: Cut the connection when pressure ignores a boundary.
block.fact: Persistent pressure after a no is a red flag. Blocking stops the channel.

move.question: She already said no twice. Next?

options.text: Explain her feelings one more time
options.feedback: They already ignored her. More explaining rarely helps.

options.text: Block the account and tell someone she trusts
options.feedback: Boundary + backup. That’s the safe combo.

options.text: Mute notifications but leave the chat open
options.feedback: Quieter, but they can still message. Blocking is stronger.

report.context: They ask for live location and offer a ride home.
report.clue: Tell the platform (and an adult) when location + control show up.
report.fact: Live location + a stranger’s car is an isolation tactic. Reporting creates a record.

options.text: Nothing — reporting makes them angrier
options.feedback: Their reaction isn’t her job. Reporting protects her and others.

options.text: Screenshots of the ask, username, and what they wanted
options.feedback: Evidence helps. Then tell a trusted adult too.

options.text: Only the username, no screenshots
options.feedback: Username helps, but screenshots show what they actually asked for.

lures.context: “Free gifts + VIP party if you come tonight. Don’t tell anyone.”
lures.clue: A bait offer that sounds too good and too urgent.
lures.fact: Gifts, exclusivity, and secrecy are classic recruitment lures.

move.question: The gifts sound real. What now?

options.text: Go with a friend so it’s “safer”
options.feedback: Bringing a friend doesn’t make a stranger’s secret party safe.

options.text: Skip it and show the invite to an adult
options.feedback: Refusing the lure and looping in help is the right call.

options.text: Ask what the gifts are first
options.feedback: Details won’t fix secrecy + urgency. Still don’t go.

isolate.context: “Your friends are jealous. Stop hanging with them — you have me.”
isolate.clue: Pulling someone away from their real support.
isolate.fact: Cutting Mary off from friends makes her easier to control. That’s isolation.

options.text: Spend less time with friends to keep the chat happy
options.feedback: That’s exactly what isolation wants.

options.text: Keep her friends close and tell them what’s going on
options.feedback: Support network first. Isolation loses power when friends know.

options.text: Stay friends but hide the chat from them
options.feedback: Keeping friends helps — hiding the chat still leaves her alone with the risk.

debt.context: They bought her a game pass, then said “ur gonna owe me one.”
debt.fact: Favours that create “you owe me” are a debt trap — gifts shouldn’t come with IOUs.

move.question: She already accepted the pass. Now?

options.text: Do one small favour so it’s even
options.feedback: That teaches them the trap works. She owes nothing.

options.text: Say she doesn’t owe them, then block if they push
options.feedback: Clear refusal. Gifts don’t buy compliance.

options.text: Offer to pay them back in money later
options.feedback: Paying can still keep the tie alive. Better to refuse the debt frame entirely.

exit.context: Mary’s stomach drops. The chat feels wrong and she’s alone online.
exit.clue: Leave the situation before it gets worse.
exit.fact: Having an exit — close the chat, leave the place, get to safety — matters more than being polite.

options.text: Keep talking until she’s sure it’s dangerous
options.feedback: Waiting for certainty costs time. Discomfort is enough reason to leave.

options.text: Stop the chat, go somewhere safe, tell an adult
options.feedback: Exit first, explain later. That’s the plan.

options.text: Log out but check back in an hour
options.feedback: Logging out helps — but telling someone beats checking alone later.

verify.context: A “job offer” lands in her DMs with a link and a contract PDF.
verify.clue: Check if it’s real before sharing anything.
verify.fact: Links and PDFs are easy to fake. Verify through a known adult or official channel — never through the stranger.

move.question: Where should Mary check the offer?

options.text: Click the link they sent — it’s faster
options.feedback: Their link can be malware or a phishing page. Don’t.

options.text: Ask a teacher/parent and look up the company separately
options.feedback: Independent check + adult help. That’s real verification.

options.text: Ask the sender for a phone number
options.feedback: Numbers can be fake too. Still verify offline with someone she trusts.

consent.context: They joke “send it anyway” after Mary already said she’s not comfortable.
consent.clue: A clear yes — pressure after a no doesn’t count.
consent.fact: Consent is ongoing and can be withdrawn. Pushing after a no is coercion, not romance.

move.question: Mary already said no. They keep joking about it.

options.text: Laugh it off so things don’t get awkward
options.feedback: Awkward is safer than giving in. Her no still stands.

options.text: Repeat the no, then leave the chat if they continue
options.feedback: Firm boundary, then exit. That’s consent in action.

options.text: Change the subject and hope they forget
options.feedback: Subject-change can help short-term, but a clear no + exit is stronger.

pressure.context: “If you delete me you’ll regret it. Everyone will see.”
pressure.clue: Threats used to force a choice.
pressure.fact: Threats, guilt, and “everyone will see” are pressure/coercion — often tied to sextortion.

options.text: Pay or send what they want so it stops
options.feedback: Paying usually makes it worse. Don’t send anything.

options.text: Stop replying, screenshot, tell an adult / helpline
options.feedback: No reply, evidence, help. That’s the safe sequence.

options.text: Argue that they’re wrong
options.feedback: Arguing keeps the chat alive. Silence + help is better.
